passage:
"Look at her. Twenty-one, like me. Perfect skin, a flat in Goa, a job she loves."
"Sarita, it's midnight. Put the phone down."
"No, look, Rashmi. And the ad right under it: 'Glass skin in 14 days.' I'm ordering it."
"You said your skin was fine last week."
"That was before I saw this. I feel like I'm so behind. Everyone's living a life and I'm in a hostel eating instant noodles."
"Zoom into her hand."
"...Why is the door frame bending?"
"Because the photo is edited. Half of what you're looking at doesn't exist."
"But the serum..."
"The serum ad sits under the edited photo on purpose. First they make you feel behind, then they sell you the fix."
Sarita put the phone face down.
"I still feel a bit rubbish."
"I know. Come make chai with me."

qa.q: What does the serum ad promise?
qa.a: The serum ad promises "Glass skin in 14 days".

qa.q: What is Sarita feeling while scrolling?
qa.a: Sarita feels behind and insecure, saying everyone else is living a life while Sarita is stuck in a hostel eating noodles.

qa.q: What helped Sarita step back from ordering?
qa.a: Rashmi got Sarita to zoom in on the bent door frame, which showed the photo was edited, and named how the ad was placed to use that feeling.

qa.q: How does Rashmi see the post differently from Sarita?
qa.a: Rashmi sees the post and ad as a sales pair that first creates a feeling of lack and then offers the fix, rather than as a real life to measure against.

grounding: A young adult comparing their life to edited photos feels behind and nearly buys a serum, until Rashmi shows how the ad uses that insecurity.

passage:
I spent most of last winter feeling like my life was a draft and everyone else's was the final copy.
Every morning I scrolled through people my age with white bedsheets, sunlit desks and planners full of neat handwriting. Under almost every post there was an ad: the lamp, the linen, the planner. By January I had bought all three. My room still looked like my room. I felt worse, like even the fix hadn't worked on me.
Then Naveen from my design class sent me two photos of his own desk: one "for posting", with warm light and one plant carefully placed, and one real, with chargers and a cold cup of tea.
"Same desk," he wrote. "Ten minutes apart."
I laughed for the first time in weeks. The planner is now half empty. The lamp is nice, honestly.
Pooja

qa.q: What three things did the narrator buy by January?
qa.a: Pooja bought the lamp, the linen and the planner.

qa.q: How did Pooja feel after buying all three things?
qa.a: Pooja felt disappointed and even lower than before, as if even the fix had failed, because the room still did not look like the posts.

qa.q: What was the turning point that changed how Pooja saw the posts?
qa.a: Naveen's two photos of the same desk, one set up for posting and one real, showed how much the polished images were staged.

qa.q: Why might Naveen have chosen to share his own messy desk?
qa.a: Naveen likely wanted to show Pooja that the perfect images are arranged, and sharing his own real desk made that point kindly without a lecture.

grounding: A young adult feels behind after polished lifestyle posts with ads beneath them, buys the products, and feels no better until shown how posts are staged.
